pdf_claim: A farm wall, built by local farmers before the battle, originally about 2-3 ft high, forms the 80-yd right-angle wall held by Webb's brigade at the Angle; the Copse of trees was under ten feet high in 1863; the wall is present at frame one; any added rail or earth reinforcement is unverified and must be flagged.
corrected_claim: The wall itself is documented and pre-existing as a farm wall (the NPS calls it 'a low stone wall that divided the Leister and Frey properties' and 'the farm boundary wall'); it stood at 6.30 a.m. on 2 Jul, when Webb put the 69th Pennsylvania behind it, and was held by the 69th and 71st Pennsylvania with Cushing's battery on 3 Jul. Two statements of the row are wrong or unsafe as printed. (1) Reinforcement is not 'unverified': Hancock's report says the 69th and 71st stood 'behind a low stone wall and a slight breastwork hastily constructed by them', Haskell (3 Jul) says the men had 'patched it with rails from the neighboring fences, and with earth', and the NPS study (Georg 1981, citing the Comte de Paris and a 20th Massachusetts account) says earth was thrown over or against the wall and rails stood on top. The additions are infantry work built after 6.30 a.m. on 2 Jul and before the assault on 3 Jul (no clock is given), the wall under them is never animated as construction. (2) The 80-yd length of the right-angle return is not stated by any source: Haskell has 'about twenty or thirty yards', Bachelder (1870, 1873) 'fifty yards', and the Philadelphia Brigade address of 1891 'some two hundred and sixty feet' (87 yd); nothing reads 80. Height: no source reads 2-3 ft: a Confederate officer wrote 'about three feet' at the Angle but 4.5-5 ft where the wall was unbroken; Haskell says the wall was badly pulled down in places and low enough to make men kneel. The Copse: a participant says the oaks 'rose but little above my horse's head' and the NPS study reasons 'not more than eight to ten feet high' (inferred); the Stone Sentinels page (blocked host) was not read. A gateway or opening in the wall to the left of the 69th Pennsylvania is documented (NPS, from a 69th Pennsylvania man's letter of 1886): the wall is not continuous.

corrected_claim: Documented: stone walls on East Cemetery Hill held by Harris's Second Brigade, First Division, XI Corps: late on 1 Jul Harris took 'a stone wall on the right, and nearly at right angles with the Baltimore road'; on 2 Jul the 75th Ohio and 17th Connecticut stood at a stone wall (Harris's first report puts it 'south of the hill', an unresolved tension); at 7 p.m. on 2 Jul the 17th Connecticut was ordered 'behind a stone wall on each side of a lane, below the battery opposite the cemetery entrance' and later changed front 'behind a wall running at right angles with the one we had just occupied'; after the repulse Harris held 'the stone wall in the rear of and parallel with' the first with his left on the Baltimore road, and before day on 3 Jul moved right along the wall to join the First Brigade. The name Brickyard Lane and the lane walls are documented only by the NPS (captions of 1863 photographs: a stone wall and stone-and-rider panels along the east side of Brickyard Lane, viewed from East Cemetery Hill; a second wall dividing Study Field 1 and Menchy Field 2 'partly dismantled and relocated for defense works'). Corrections to the 2026-11-04 row: R247 is Maj. A. G. Brady of the 17th CONNECTICUT, a regiment of Harris's own brigade (not the 25th Ohio of 'the other brigade'); so the lane walls are held by Harris's brigade, not by von Gilsa's. No report places von Gilsa's First Brigade on a lane: its 41st New York sat behind a 'square stone fence' at the cemetery to the right of the Baltimore road (P-03). That the lane of Brady's report is Brickyard Lane is an inference (no source names both). Pre-existing farm walls: the NPS says the walls of the area are farm walls (dry-laid, from field clearing, property boundaries) and that battle modifications existed; no source names the builder or date of these walls; the photograph reading shows rubble lines of irregular height.

corrected_claim: The wall is documented, but not by the passage the 2026-11-04 row used. Patterson's 88th Pennsylvania was 'drawn up in line of battle along a stone fence' after a two-mile march from Emmitsburg (about noon): that fence is an unplaced halt, not the Oak Ridge wall, and is withdrawn as its evidence. The Oak Ridge wall is stated by three other witnesses: Rodes says Iverson's brigade 'suffered very heavily from the enemy's musketry fire from behind a stone wall along the crest of the ridge', Iverson that the enemy was 'strongly posted in woods and behind a concealed stone wall', and Col. Prey (104th New York, Paul's brigade) that Confederates 'strongly posted behind a stone wall covered with thick underbrush' were driven from it by his left companies, after which he took position behind the same wall; Col. Wheelock (97th New York, Baxter's brigade) says his skirmishers drew fire from a stone wall and the embankment of the road. The NPS Cultural Landscape Report (First Day) says Baxter's and Paul's brigades were 'hidden in part behind the overgrown and tumbled-down stone walls along the east boundary of the Forney Farm', entrenched along the stone walls on Oak Ridge to the Mummasburg Road, and built additional breastworks of fence rails; by 2.00 p.m. they had formed the new line. corrected_claim: Documented in part and contradicted in the schedule's framing. Fences and walls stood on all three grounds: post-and-rail and post-and-plank fences stood on the line of the Confederate advance on 3 Jul and had to be climbed (Peyton: three high post-and-rail fences; Shepard: 'a lane inclosed by two stout post and plank fences', 'a very great obstruction'; Davis: 'a strong post and rail fence' and others like it), and the NPS reads post-and-rail fences on both sides of the road (Klingel farm front). Stone fences and walls stood around the Wheatfield (Sweitzer, Crawford, Burbank, Brooke, de Trobriand, Kershaw) and fences stood at the Peach Orchard and the Sherfy buildings on the afternoon of 2 Jul (3rd Maine, 110th and 114th Pennsylvania, Thompson's battery). But the fences were not intact when the battle came and the seed schedule's 'present at frame one, destruction in B.8.7' needs a Jul 2 morning state: after midnight and on the morning of 2 Jul the Third Corps cleared fences and walls in its front to the Emmitsburg Road (Bodine, 26th Pennsylvania: 'detailed to clear away the fences in front of the division'; Higgins: at 10 a.m. Ward ordered 'all stone walls and fences in our front to the Emmitsburg road' demolished, done by about 11 a.m.; Humphreys: communication made easy by 'removing such of the fences as were in the way'; NPS: many north-south fences removed before the second day, 'enough were standing on July 2-3 to hinder orderly troop movement'); about 4 p.m. on 2 Jul two regiments of Harrow's brigade 'tore down the fences and constructed breastworks' along the Emmitsburg Road (Gibbon; Joslin's 15th Massachusetts built 'a small breastwork of rails behind the fence'; Hancock: 'a slight breastwork of such materials as the adjoining fences afforded'). 'Double post-and-rail on both sides along the whole road' is not supported for the whole road: it is documented for the Klingel front and Shepard's lane, and the sources show gaps (removed segments, thrown-down openings). Per-segment type and height are not given; Savas-Hessler and the Gettysburg Daily page (GD-EmmRd) are blocked hosts.

pdf_claim: The unfinished railroad grade and cut on McPherson Ridge is an earlier excavation, used for cover about 11:00 on 1 Jul; it is modelled as terrain, not construction; the cut dimensions are an open gap.
corrected_claim: The grade and cut are documented as pre-existing, as the PDF says, and the 'cut dimensions' gap is partly filled; the hour is not a reported time. Pre-existing: the Park Service Cultural Landscape Report says the Gettysburg Railroad (the 'Tapeworm Railroad') built a level grade in 1838, the company failed before track was laid, and the local community used the grade as a wagon road; a short distance north of the Chambersburg pike the grade ran parallel to the turnpike, with cuts through the ridges: the first through the diabase bedrock of Seminary Ridge, 'followed by two smaller cuts through two branches of McPherson Ridge'. The Official Records call it 'the railroad grading' or 'railroad cut' (Doubleday: parallel to the Cashtown road and about 100 yards from it; Hall: a road he could not leave 'from its construction'); the New York state book calls it 'an unfinished railroad grade' with 'a deep cut, whose steep, rocky sides afforded no opportunity for escape'. Used for cover on 1 Jul: by the Confederates of Davis's brigade, who 'flung his troops into the railroad cut for safety' when the 6th Wisconsin, 95th New York and 14th Brooklyn charged (Doubleday; Dawes: 'their cover in the cut', 'the rebels began throwing down their arms'; the NPS: 'sought cover from heavy fire of the 6th Wisconsin in the deep railroad cut (second cut)'), and by Union troops: the 149th Pennsylvania, ordered by Col. Stone to 'take possession of the railroad cut, about 50 paces to my front', lay in it 'their arms resting on the bank' (Dwight), with the cut 'about 100 yards from the road' (Stone) and 'in front' of the line (Irvin); Daniel's North Carolinians took the cut later. The NPS calls the cut a 'ready-made entrenchment ... for cover and concealment'. Dimensions, no longer wholly open: depth is documented at two places and the values differ: the NPS Cultural Landscape Report gives an '18-foot-deep battle-era railroad cut through McPherson Ridge' (where Reynolds Avenue crosses; the Second Railroad Cut 'remains largely unchanged since 1863'), while Dawes (1890) found it 'four feet deep' where he stood at the edge. Length, width and profile are in no source. Distance: 100 yards from the road (Stone, Irvin), 50 paces in front of the 149th (Dwight), 175 paces from the turnpike fence to the cut (Dawes). Hour: no Official Records report gives a time for the cut fight or for the 6th Wisconsin's charge; the row's 'about 11:00' is inferred (see timeline_corrections tl-02 T1-108, which bounds it before about 11:30 from Howard's watch) and the Union occupation by the 149th Pennsylvania belongs to a later phase (Dwight has Ewell's attack on the Eleventh Corps and a brigade advancing on his front).

A second negative, LC-B811-63A and 63B (cwpb-00712 and 00713, 'Meade's Hdqs. Gettysburg, Pa.', undated: 'between 1861 and 1869', not attributed to Gardner), shows a longer wall of rounded stones across the foreground with a farm lane and broken rails beside it. The Park Service's Record of Treatment uses the same Gardner file (cwpb 00887) for the east-boundary stone wall of Frey Field 5 and says that 'the battle accounts of the 14th Connecticut and historic imagery from 1863 and the 1880s indicate a stone wall stood on the eastern edge of the Leister Field 4 and not a stone and rider fence'. State: by the time of the July photographs the wall by the gate is largely tumbled and the Park Service says 'the house and surrounding fences are all damaged' (the shelling of 3 Jul overshot the ridge onto the farm); no source gives the hour or the cause of the damage to the wall. corrected_claim: The Company B wall is documented as used and, by the Park Service, as pre-existing; the PDF's two walls are probably one wall; the 150 yards is unsupported; and the reasoning 'used, not built' does not carry over to the other walls of Little Round Top and Round Top, which the Official Records say were built. Used: Capt. Morrill of Company B, 20th Maine, wrote on 8 Jul 1863 that, having reached 'the left of the woods', he 'found some twelve or fifteen U.S. Sharpshooters under the command of a non-commissioned officer', who asked to stay under his command, and 'we took position behind a stone wall there'; when the enemy appeared on the right and the regiment charged, they fired and called out 'to charge' (the Park Service quotes the letter; the Park Service places the position east of Little Round Top, and a Tipton photograph of 1898 shows the wall behind the Company B marker). Maine at Gettysburg (1898) puts Morrill's skirmishers, with 2nd U.S. Sharpshooters, 'behind a stone-wall, on the right of the 15th Ala.', where the company 'occupied a stone-wall in the rear of the position taken up by the enemy' and fired a volley into the rear. Chamberlain's own report (OR p.623-624) names no wall: Company B was 'detached ... to extend from my left flank across this hollow as a line of skirmishers', and Morrill with 'some dozen or fifteen of the U. S. Sharpshooters' fell on the enemy 'as they were breaking'. Pre-existing: the Park Service's Cultural Landscapes Inventory lists the 'Field Stone Wall, Jacob Weikert Farm / Company B, 20th Maine Stone Wall (built pre-1863)', a north-south wall just east of Vincent Spur next to the Company B marker, today 'around 135 feet long and 2 feet high' (a modern survey, not an 1863 profile), and says the nearby Weikert woods lane 'was present during the battle and likely used by the Union army, as the Company B stone wall was nearby'; it lists the wall among the 'existing stone fences' that 'become integral parts of the battlefield' in 1863. No 1863 text says who built it. The sharpshooters' wall and the Company B wall are the same place in Morrill's letter ('we took position behind a stone wall there'); a second wall 'about 150 yd east of Little Round Top' is in no source read. Not generalisable: the Official Records document stone walls built on this ground: Garrard (Weed's brigade) 'At night this ridge, naturally strong, was strengthened by building a stone wall about half way down the slope, wherever the rocks offered no protection to the men'; Chamberlain 'Rude shelters were thrown up of the loose rocks'; Fisher, on the morning of 3 Jul, 'at once threw up a stone wall across the entire ravine and up the hill' between the two hills; the Park Service records 'defensive stone walls built along the summit of Little Round Top and at Vincent Spur' and a veteran of the 140th New York who 'built stone walls in the dark'. The earlier note's use of Capt. D. P. Hancock (7th U.S.) as a Round Top wall is withdrawn: his 'stone fence inclosing a wood' lies at the Wheatfield (P-04).

corrected_claim: Confirmed with additions and one correction of time. The Twelfth Corps artillery that fired on Culp's Hill on the morning of 3 Jul stood on two heights and by the Baltimore pike. Knap's Pennsylvania battery (Lt. Atwell; six 10-pounder Parrotts) was 'placed on a knob situated southwest of the pike 100 yards from it, and known on that day as Slocum's Hill' (Muhlenberg), 'on the hill known as Slocum's headquarters, and near the Baltimore pike' (Hunt); Winegar's Battery M, 1st New York (four 10-pounders) stood 'on a second elevation, a quarter of a mile distant, and nearly due east' (Muhlenberg), 'at a short distance east of it' (Hunt); both overlooked the ground the corps had left and stayed there through the whole engagement. Muhlenberg's F, 4th U.S. (six 12-pounders) and Kinzie's K, 5th U.S. (four 12-pounders) were put in position at 1 a.m. on 3 Jul on the southwest side of the pike opposite the centre of the corps line. Hunt adds a fifth battery, Rigby's A, Maryland (six 3-inch), 'placed on the hill' soon after daylight; Rigby himself puts his battery on a hill about a mile south of Gettysburg and 500 yards west of the pike and says he shelled the woods from daylight for about three hours (Tyler: by Slocum's direction). The Official Records never use the name Powers Hill. Sources outside the OR do: 'Powers' Hill is where General Slocum had his head-quarters' (Bachelder 1873, who adds that the Twelfth Corps batteries were sent to Powers' and Culp's hills); the 1940 National Park Service study, following the Comte de Paris, puts Knap's on Power's Hill and Winegar's on McAllister's Hill, a quarter of a mile apart; the Park Service's 1999 General Management Plan says 'Before 4 a.m., Twelfth Corps artillery at Powers Hill and along the Baltimore Pike opened fire against Confederate positions on the south slope and ridge of Culp's Hill'. The history of Battery M (1889) differs: its right section stood on Powers' Hill and its left on the McAllister farm hill. Opening clock: 3.30 a.m. (Geary), 3.45 (Candy), 4.00 (Slocum, Greene, Packer: 'twenty pieces'), 4.30 (Muhlenberg, Hunt), 'daylight' (Williams); the first fire lasted ten minutes (Geary) or fifteen (Muhlenberg, Hunt, Williams); all the batteries fired at intervals from 5.30 to about 10 a.m. (Muhlenberg, Hunt). Guns: 20 (Muhlenberg, Packer) or 26 with Rigby (Hunt). No work (earthwork, gun pit, epaulement) is described for any of these batteries in any text read: the PDF's 'not described' stands. Meade's move is documented but belongs to the afternoon cannonade, not to the morning fire: the Leister farmhouse was hit (a shell burst among the staff horses tied to the fence), Meade and staff withdrew to the fenced yard behind the house, headquarters then moved to a barn several hundred yards down the Taneytown Road, and after a shell struck Butterfield there Meade and staff 'removed to General Slocum's head-quarters on Powers Hill' (Meade's son, 1913; also Toombs 1888 and New York at Gettysburg 1900). The cannonade opened at 1 p.m. and lasted about three hours (Meade's own dispatch). 'Untenable' is the PDF's word: the sources say the house was too exposed and that no staff officer could reach headquarters from the corps commanders; the Park Service Leister page says only that Meade 'evacuated to a new headquarters'.

(1) 'Not described' is contradicted for Stevens' Knoll and the batteries by the cemetery gate: Hunt writes of the evening of 1 Jul that 'each of the guns in these batteries had a small earthwork thrown up in its front'; Whittier (5th Maine): 'During the night, temporary earthworks were thrown up covering the pieces'; Bachelder 1873: 'The redans thrown up to protect the guns can still be seen'; Maine at Gettysburg 1898: 'The earthworks thrown up on the night of July first for the protection of the men and pieces have been preserved'; the Park Service calls them Stevens Knoll Lunettes, reconstructed 1880-90, and a 1940 survey measured the restacked lunettes at 30 inches (never an 1863 profile). The works were built on the night of 1 Jul, so they are prepared works built on screen (the same class as G-03), not pre-existing. (2) The batteries that opened at about 04:00 on 3 Jul are not the knoll's: they are the Twelfth Corps artillery near Slocum's headquarters hill and the Baltimore pike (G-17: four batteries named by Slocum and Muhlenberg, five with Rigby's on Hunt's account). What the OR documents at Stevens' Knoll is: Wainwright commanded the batteries north of the Baltimore pike in front of the cemetery gate (from the evening of 1 Jul, Hunt); on 3 Jul Hunt lists five of them from right to left: Stevens' (5th Maine, six guns; OCR '13-pounders', 12-pounders on p.231), Reynolds' (four 3-inch), Ricketts' (six 3-inch), Wiedrich's (four 3-inch) and Stewart's (four 12-pounders): 24 guns. So 'five batteries' and 'Wainwright commanded' are both documented, by Hunt. The 5th Maine's own morning fire has no hour: Whittier has the battery open 'on the morning of the 3d' at 1,500 yards on columns of infantry 'on advice received from General Ames', and fire for an hour on an enemy battery; Wainwright has 'occasional shots at bodies of the enemy's troops in the distance during the morning' (so '04:00' is the Twelfth Corps clock and is not documented for the knoll). The name Stevens' Knoll is post-battle: 'Since the battle that knoll has been named Stevens' Knoll or Hill' (Maine 1898); the OR says 'a small knoll', 'the knoll to the right and rear of Cemetery Hill'. A 1940 Park Service study also puts two Federal batteries on Culp's Hill itself with no lunettes; no OR report read places a battery on Culp's Hill proper.
